vignette:
He comes to session straight from the job site, the dust still clinging to the creases of his work pants. He sits on the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees, fingers drumming a quiet rhythm against the denim. He is forty-one, single, a construction worker who has spent twenty years building walls for other people while trying not to think about the ones that fell around him as a boy.

He remembers the first time clearly, though he wishes he didn't. He was six, maybe seven, in the kitchen of the small apartment in Amman. His mother was washing dishes, his father came home late. The argument started low, then rose like a tide. He learned to read the pitch of his father's voice the way a weatherman reads a barometer-except he could never run fast enough. That night his father's hand connected with his mother's cheek. The sound was sharp, wet. She didn't cry, not then. She just held the side of her face and turned back to the sink. He stood in the doorway, frozen, his small fingers pressed into the doorframe. He didn't say a word. He never did.

The violence became the background hum of his childhood. Some nights his mother would send him to his room before it started; other nights she couldn't. He learned to make himself very small, to hold his breath, to listen for the thuds and the stifled gasps. He never intervened-his father was a large man, and the few times he tried, he was shoved aside. So he watched. He watched his mother's swollen lip at breakfast. He watched her explain away a bruise as a fall. He watched his father laugh with neighbors at dinner as if nothing had happened. And he never told anyone. Not his teachers, not his friends, not the imam. The silence became a second skin.

He left Jordan at nineteen, came to the United States alone. He found work in construction-the physical labor felt honest, it exhausted his body so his mind had less room to wander. He builds now, high-rises mostly. He's good with his hands, precise, reliable. But there are triggers he cannot name. The sound of a dropped hammer in a stairwell-a sudden clang-and his chest tightens, his vision narrows. He has to set down his tools, walk outside, breathe until the world stops spinning. He tells the foreman it's dust in his lungs. More than once he has snapped at a coworker who touched him from behind, spinning around with fists raised before he recognized the face. The shame follows him home.

Nights are hardest. He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment. He sleeps with the light on-has done so since childhood. He starts awake at the smallest noise: a neighbor's door slamming, a car backfiring. His heart hammers, his palms sweat, and for a long minute he is six years old again, listening for his father's footsteps. He is irritable and withdrawn. He has not had a serious relationship in years. Women find him distant, guarded. He knows this. He wants to be close, but when someone raises their voice in anger, even at a football game on TV, his stomach knots and he has to leave the room.

He does not drink heavily, does not use drugs. He works, he pays his bills, he watches old satellite reruns of Jordanian soap operas until he falls into a restless sleep. He told his primary care doctor he had trouble sleeping, was given a prescription for a mild sedative. He never filled it. He doesn't trust medicine. He doesn't trust much.

He came to therapy because his foreman noticed him flinch at a loud noise and suggested he "talk to someone." He didn't argue. He doesn't know how to talk about this, but he knows the weight of carrying it alone. In session he speaks in fragments, eyes on the floor. He describes the kitchen, the sound of his mother's breath when she was hit. He says, "I am still in that doorway. I never left."
